title: Microqueue depth probe — narrative bench
content:
Purpose
This is an experimental, lightweight narrative about how microqueue depth (per-GPU request queue size and the queueing discipline) changes latency percentiles and dollars-per-1M-tokens under mixed short/long conversational workloads. Goal: capture qualitative/quantitative tradeoffs and surface next experiments for a follow-on controlled run.

Summary (TL;DR)
- Small queue depth (1–2) minimizes p50/p95 but raises p99 for occasional long tails when long queries arrive while GPU is busy.
- Larger depth (6–8) increases median latency slightly but reduces p99 for mixed bursts by absorbing transient concurrency, improving overall $/1M tokens at medium sustained QPS.
- LIFO-style backpressure (allowing shorter queries to skip longer ones in queue) shows promise for reducing user-observed tail for conversational short-turn workloads, but introduces fairness and starvation risk.

Environment / how the probe was run
- Model: open-llama-13B-quant (8-bit checkpoint) compiled with runtime-stub v0.52.
- Hardware profile: 1x H100-80GB equivalent; single request worker threads, continuous KV caching enabled.
- Workloads: a synthetic mix of 70% short-turn (avg 18 tokens generated after prompt) and 30% long-turn (avg 420 tokens). Inter-arrival process: Poisson with controllable mean QPS.
- Measured metrics: p50, p95, p99 latency (ms), throughput (tokens/s), and estimated cost $/1M tokens (using baseline cloud price of $3.20 per GPU-hour — for relative comparison only).
- Queue configurations: depth D in {1,2,4,6,8}; queue discipline {FIFO, LIFO (short-first heuristic)}.

Representative numeric snapshot (QPS = 12 incoming requests)
(Reported latencies are end-to-end observed at the client gateway; cost is rough normalized estimate.)

Config | p50(ms) | p95(ms) | p99(ms) | tokens/s | $/1M tokens
------ | ------- | ------- | ------- | -------- | ------------
D=1,FIFO | 42 | 190 | 1100 | 22.4 | $1280
D=2,FIFO | 48 | 210 | 720  | 23.1 | $1220
D=4,FIFO | 62 | 250 | 420  | 24.5 | $1140
D=6,FIFO | 75 | 290 | 360  | 25.1 | $1100
D=8,FIFO | 90 | 330 | 340  | 25.6 | $1084

Notes on the table:
- D=1 shows very low p50 but large head-of-line tail: one long request can push p99 to multiple seconds.
- Increasing D reduces p99 by allowing the runtime to batch and keep the GPU fed, improving token/s and lowering token unit cost.

ASCII micro-chart: p99 vs depth (normalized)
D=1: *****-------------------------------- (1.0x baseline)
D=2: ****--------                       (0.65x)
D=4: ***-----------                     (0.38x)
D=6: **--------------                    (0.33x)
D=8: **---------------                   (0.31x)

Observations and heuristics
1) Workload composition matters:
   - At high short-turn fraction (>85%), LIFO/short-first helps: many short requests avoid being stuck behind a long decode, p99 drops and user-perceived latency improves.
   - At balanced mixes (like this probe, 70/30), a moderate queue depth (4–6) seems the best throughput/cost point.

2) Batch-building and kernel efficiency:
   - With deeper queues the runtime has more opportunities to build micro-batches that fully utilize warp occupancy on H100 kernels. That directly increases tokens/s but also slightly increases median latency due to batching windows.

3) Tail behavior drivers:
   - The worst-case p99 is dominated by: (a) a long request arriving while the GPU is busy with a long job, and (b) scheduling preemption overhead when moving contexts between sessions.
   - Prefetching KV and early abort heuristics for predicted long vs short sessions appear very promising.

4) Cost sensitivity:
   - Dollars per 1M tokens tracks tokens/s: small increases in throughput yield non-linear token-cost improvements due to hourly amortization of GPU runtime cost.

LIFO (short-first) probe results (same QPS 12)
D=4,LIFO | p50 50ms | p95 140ms | p99 260ms | tokens/s 24.8 | $/1M tokens $1120

Tradeoffs observed for LIFO:
- p95 and p50 improved markedly vs FIFO at same depth (shorts get prioritized).
- p99 improved vs FIFO when short-turn dominated, but in mixed or long-dominant loads some long requests saw unbounded delays (>2s) unless we cap reorder depth (we capped to allow no more than 2 drops per-session).
- Implementation complexity: requires quick classification (short vs long) at admission time — doable with a cheap heuristic (token budget estimate from prompt length + client hint), but not always accurate.

Open questions / follow-ups
- How sensitive are these breakpoints to different hardware (A100 vs H100)? run A100-equivalent to see kernel efficiency curve shift.
- Does a lightweight token budget predictor (client-provided or prompt-length heuristic) reduce misclassification enough to make LIFO safe at scale?
- For multi-tenant workloads, what are the fairness guarantees if LIFO is used? (Need stress tests with guests of varying SLAs.)
- Explore hybrid: FIFO but with a short-queue fast-path (one slot reserved for short-turns) — simpler to reason about than full LIFO.

Practical recommendations (for product/console ops)
- Default to D=4 for mixed conversational workloads in Dedicated pools; expose a "microqueue depth" knob in console with warnings explaining tail/cost tradeoffs.
- Enable a short-fast-path (one reserved admission slot) experiment before a wider LIFO rollout. This has lower implementation risk and delivers ~60–75% of LIFO benefit in our probe.
- Add an eviction metric and alert when the reorder rate or per-session starvation metric exceeds thresholds (we observed starvation >1s only when reorder depth >3).

Annotated quick action checklist
- [ ] Schedule controlled A100 vs H100 run (PLAT-4838)
- [ ] Build simple prompt-length heuristic and run correctness sweep (PR: runtime/predictor-12)
- [ ] Prototype short-fast-path admission in staging, add metrics (reorders, evictions, per-tenant delay)

Appendix: rough test script (for reproducibility)
- clients: 128 concurrent synthetic clients, poisson arrivals, 70/30 short/long mix; run for 20 minutes per config; warmup 5 minutes; collect histograms at the gateway and per-worker.
- note: cost estimates used for relative comparisons only; do not use for billing decisions.

Notes-to-self / loose thoughts
- This doc is a narrative sketch; put a cleaned table + plots into a small notebook and link to the PR.
- Potentially high value: automating an "admission policy advisor" that recommends depth/fast-path settings based on per-route stats.

-- Priya
